title: Consistent Hashing
concept: Consistent hashing places both servers and keys on the same hash ring and assigns each key to the next server along it. When a server joins or leaves, only the keys next to it move, instead of nearly all of them as with hash-mod-N. That stability is what lets caches and stateful services grow and shrink without a mass reshuffle, though a ring with few servers spreads load unevenly unless each server takes many points on it.

posts.title: Saving another 100TB of RAM with math (and Rust)

digest.problem: Cloudflare routes cacheable requests to servers by URL with consistent hashing, so each data center keeps one copy of each file. Its internal load balancer builds these rings with the open-source pingora-ketama library, and an engineer flagged that the rings were using far too much memory, reaching about 6GB in some cases.
digest.constraints: Every service runs on every machine, so wasted memory is multiplied across the fleet. With one point per server the ring is badly uneven, so each server gets many points, and weighting servers by disk size multiplies the count further. Compliance and caching features restrict which servers may handle a request, so each feature combination needs its own ring. Any change to a ring moves cached files and sends extra traffic to customers' origin servers, so the rollout had to be careful and reversible.

walkthrough.explanation: They worked out how unevenly load spreads with one point per server and how adding points shrinks that spread, with sharply diminishing returns.
A ring entry went from 8 bytes to 6 by storing a 16-bit server index instead of 32-bit, saved as a raw byte array because Rust's alignment padding otherwise kept it at 8.
Guided by the math, they cut the points generated per server by 90%, where the measured loss of balance was negligible.
The load balancer kept the old and new rings side by side and chose one per request, which made rollback instant.
The change went data center by data center, small locations first, with traffic share and location controlled separately.
Once the migration reached 100%, the old ring was removed.

tradeoffs.chosen: Far fewer points per server, a smaller entry layout, and a slow rollout by data center with both rings running side by side.
tradeoffs.rejected: Keeping the default point counts, forcing a packed struct layout, and switching every data center at once.
tradeoffs.why: The math showed most points bought almost no extra balance while costing memory on every machine. A global switch would have invalidated most cached content at once and flooded origins, so they accepted a slower rollout and temporary double memory.

digest.failures: Changing only the index type saved nothing because of alignment padding. Adding ever more points stopped paying off: each step down in error needs roughly ten times more points, and with 32-bit hashes, collisions at high point counts actually add error. Separate rings per feature combination grow quickly, so more points could never solve that part.
digest.takeaways: Check defaults like 160 points per server against the math, because small per-server costs become huge at fleet scale. Measure where returns diminish before assuming more is better. For anything that decides cache placement, roll out gradually with independent control over traffic share and location, and keep a way back.

posts.title: How Discord Scaled Elixir to 5,000,000 Concurrent Users
posts.ageNote: A 2017 account. It is here for a fundamental that does not depend on Discord's current setup: on a hot read path, copying shared data can cost more than the lookup itself. Discord's ring and tooling may have changed since, and this page does not claim they are current.

digest.problem: Discord places each guild (a server, in Discord's terms) on a node chosen with a consistent hash ring, and every user session asks the ring where its guilds live. When many users reconnected at once, the single process answering ring lookups could not keep up, and the whole system overloaded.
digest.constraints: Users are in about 5 guilds on average, and one Erlang VM can hold up to 500,000 sessions, so restarting a session server means millions of lookups at once. Any call to another Erlang process costs about 12μs, which alone added up to around 30 seconds of lookups after a restart.

walkthrough.explanation: The ring began as an existing hash ring library called through an Erlang C port, owned by a single process.
Several copies of the ring in several processes would spread the load, but every lookup would still be a cross-process call on a hot path.
They rewrote the ring in pure Elixir and copied it into ETS, Erlang's shared in-memory table, so sessions could read it without messaging a process.
Finally they used mochiglobal, ported to Elixir as FastGlobal: the ring is compiled into a generated module whose constant data sits on a shared read-only heap, so reading it copies nothing.

tradeoffs.chosen: Compile the ring into a module so reads are nearly free and copy nothing.
tradeoffs.rejected: A single ring process, several ring processes, and an ETS table.
tradeoffs.why: Each rejected option still paid per lookup, either for a process hop or for copying the ring. FastGlobal makes every change to the ring slow, since the module must be regenerated, which Discord accepted because the ring is read constantly and changes rarely.

digest.failures: The C port bottlenecked on its single process. More processes would have spread the load but kept the per-call cost. ETS removed the process hop but still copied the ring on every read, which left 17.5 seconds of lookups after a restart.
digest.takeaways: On a hot read path, copying shared data can cost more than the work itself, so removing the copy can beat adding parallelism. When data is read constantly and changes rarely, make reads cheap and let writes be slow.

comparison: Both companies kept consistent hashing and attacked the cost of the ring itself, but they hit different limits. Discord's problem was lookup speed on a hot path, with every user session needing ring lookups after a restart, so it moved the ring into compiled module memory and accepted slow rebuilds because the ring rarely changes. Cloudflare's problem was memory, with dozens of large weighted rings in its load balancer, so it shrank the ring with fewer points and a tighter layout, accepting slightly less even balance and a slow rollout because any ring change moves cached files.

glossary.definition: The output range of a hash function bent into a circle, with servers and keys placed on it by their hashes.
One of several positions a single server takes on the ring, used to even out how much of the ring it owns.
The standard deviation divided by the mean, a way to say how uneven load is in percent.
Moving keys between servers after the set of servers changes.
Keeping requests for the same content on the same server, so it stays cached there.
A multiplier that gives a server more points, and so more keys, than others.

mistakes: Using hash-mod-N for a cache cluster. Changing N remaps almost every key, and the resulting misses can overwhelm the database.
Giving each server a single point on the ring. Arcs end up very uneven, so some servers carry far more keys than others.
Assuming more points is always better. Returns diminish quickly, memory grows linearly, and with 32-bit hashes collisions eventually add error back.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why hash-mod-N breaks a cache cluster when it grows or shrinks.
why.body:
A cache spread over many servers only helps if every client sends the same key to the same server. The obvious rule is to hash the key and take it modulo the number of servers.

That rule falls apart when the number changes. Add or remove one server and almost every key maps somewhere new, so almost every read becomes a miss at the same moment, and the database behind the cache takes the full load. Consistent hashing exists so that a change in the number of servers moves only a small share of keys.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture keys and servers on a ring and see which keys move.
mentalModel.body:
Hash both servers and keys onto the same circle of numbers, the ring. Each key belongs to the first server you reach going clockwise from it. When a server joins, it takes over only the keys between it and the server before it. When a server leaves, only its keys move, to the next server along.

With one point per server the arcs between servers are very uneven, so some servers own far more of the ring. The fix is to give each server many points, often called virtual nodes, which evens out the arcs at the cost of a bigger ring.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can place a key, add a server, and say what moves.

steps.explanation: Hash each server, many times with different suffixes, to put its points on the ring.
Hash the key and find the next point clockwise, usually with a binary search over the sorted points. That point's server owns the key.
Its new points take over the keys just before them. Every other key stays where it was.
Its keys pass to the next points along. Again, only those keys move.
A bigger server gets more points, so it owns more of the ring.
Every client needs the same ring, and lookups sit on the hot path, so the ring's memory and lookup cost matter.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can see what a ring costs in real systems, in memory and in lookup time.

steps.explanation: Cloudflare's math for 100 servers: with one point each, load varies by about 99%; with 160 points each, the default in NGINX and Pingora, about 8%.
Cloudflare needs a ring per combination of compliance and caching features, and points multiply with disk-size weights, so some rings reached about 6GB, on every machine.
Returns diminish sharply, so Cloudflare cut the points per server by 90% and shrank each entry from 8 bytes to 6, reclaiming over 100TB of RAM.
Every ring change moves cached files and sends traffic to origins, so both rings ran side by side and the switch went data center by data center.

In a 2017 post, Discord described its ring lookups bottlenecking on one process after a restart: about 30 seconds of lookups. Compiling the ring into a shared module cut each lookup from 12μs to 0.3μs.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid the three most common mistakes with hash rings.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: A cache cluster uses hash(key) mod N. You add one server. What happens?
options: Almost every key maps to a different server, so most reads miss
Only the new server's keys move
quiz.why: Changing N changes the result for nearly every key.
wrong: That is what consistent hashing achieves, not mod N.
The mapping depends on N, so it changes.

quiz.question: On a hash ring, which server owns a key?
options: The server with the most keys
The first server point clockwise from the key's hash
quiz.why: Every client walks clockwise to the same point, so they all agree.
wrong: Ownership depends on position, not load.
It must be the same server every time for the cache to help.

quiz.question: A server leaves the ring. Which keys move?
options: Only the keys that server owned
quiz.why: Its keys pass to the next server along; everyone else keeps theirs.
wrong: Only the departing server's share moves.

quiz.question: Why give each server many points on the ring?
options: To even out how much of the ring each server owns
quiz.why: With one point each, arcs vary wildly; many points average them out.
wrong: Points have nothing to do with encryption.
Lookups still search the sorted points.

quiz.question: Going from 160 to 1,600 points per server mostly costs you what?
options: Ten times the memory for little extra balance
quiz.why: Balance improves slowly while memory grows with the point count.
wrong: Every point takes memory on every machine.

quiz.question: Why did Discord's ring lookups take seconds after a restart?
options: The ring had too few points
Every lookup paid for a call to the single process that owned the ring
quiz.why: Millions of lookups each paying about 12μs added up to around 30 seconds.
wrong: Point count was not the bottleneck.
The cost was the process hop, not hashing.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how two companies cut the cost of a hash ring, in memory and in lookup time.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain when a ring's memory matters and when its lookup speed does.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply the concept to a cache cluster, design a ring, and plan for ten times the scale.

exercises.prompt: Every time you add a cache server, your database load spikes for an hour. The client uses hash mod N. What do you change?
exercises.answer: Switch to a consistent hash ring with many points per server, so adding a server moves only about one N-th of the keys. Add servers one at a time.
exercises.tradeoffs: The ring takes memory and every client must build it the same way.
wrongAnswers: Keeping mod N and warming the whole cache by hand.

exercises.prompt: Design how a load balancer routes cacheable URLs to servers in a data center, with servers of different disk sizes.
exercises.answer: Build a ring with points weighted by disk size, pick the point count from the balance you need rather than a default, store entries compactly, and keep one ring per set of servers allowed for a request.
exercises.tradeoffs: Fewer points means slightly less even load; separate rings per feature combination multiply memory.
wrongAnswers: Using a default point count without checking it.
Equal points for servers of different sizes.
One ring for requests that may only go to some servers.

exercises.prompt: Your fleet grows ten times and you need to change the ring's layout. How do you roll it out?
exercises.answer: Run the old and new rings side by side, choose one per request, and move traffic location by location, small sites first, with separate controls for traffic share and location. Remove the old ring only at 100%.
exercises.tradeoffs: Two rings double memory during the move, and the rollout is slow.
wrongAnswers: Switching every data center at once and flooding origins with misses.
Assuming more points will fix any imbalance.

next.outcome: After this you can pick the next topic that builds on this one.
next.body: A ring tells every client where each key lives. Sharding applies the same idea to databases, splitting data across machines by key, and it adds a new problem: moving data safely when the layout changes.
